source_text: Refugit et ipse vim interdum, sed eadem ratione qua apostolis fugere praeceperat, donec scilicet doctrinam suam impleret, qua consummata, non dico stetit, sed nec auxilium a patre angelorum exercituum desideravit, increpito etiam Petri gladio. Professus quidem et ipse est animam anxiam usque ad mortem et carnem infirmam, ut tibi ostenderet primo in se utramque substantiam humanam fuisse ex proprietate anxietatis animae et imbecillitatis carnis, ne aliam, ut quidam nunc induxerunt, aut carnem aut animam Christi interpretareris, dehinc ut demonstratis conditionibus earum scires illas nihil valere per semetipsas sine spiritu. Et ideo praeponit spiritus promptus, ut utramque conditionem substantiae utriusque respiciens intellegas in te esse etiam fortitudipem spiritus, quomodo et infirmitatem carnis, ac iam hinc scias quid unde facias et quid cui subicias, infirmum scilicet forti, ne, ut nunc facis, de carnis quidem infirmitate causeris, de spiritus autem firmitate dissimules. Postulavit et ipse a patre, si fieri posset, transiret ab illo calix passionis. Postula et tu, sed stans ut ille, sed postulans tantum, sed subiungens et reliqua, Verum non quod ego volo, sed quod tu. Fugiens autem quomodo hoc postulabis, ipse tibi praestans calicis translationem, nec quod pater vult faciens, sed quod tu?
thought_title: Christ's own example of not fleeing
orientation: Tertullian is arguing from Christ's own conduct in his passion that flight is not permitted, answering the objection that Christ himself sometimes withdrew.
pass_a_gloss: He himself also fled violence sometimes, but by the same reasoning by which he had commanded the apostles to flee, until of course he should fulfill his teaching; when that was completed, I do not say he stood, but he did not even desire help from the Father of armies of angels, after rebuking even Peter's sword. He himself indeed confessed his soul anxious even to death and his flesh weak, so that he might show you first that in himself both human substances had existed from the property of anxiety of soul and weakness of flesh, lest you should interpret either the flesh or the soul of Christ as something else, as certain people have now introduced; then so that, once the conditions of them had been demonstrated, you might know that they are worth nothing by themselves without the spirit. And therefore he puts forward the spirit as willing, so that, looking at each condition of each substance, you may understand that in you there is also strength of spirit, just as also weakness of flesh, and from this point you may know what you should do from what and what you should subject to what, namely the weak to the strong, lest, as you now do, you complain about the weakness of the flesh but ignore the firmness of the spirit. He himself also asked the Father that, if it could happen, the cup of suffering should pass from him. Ask also you, but standing as he did, but asking only, but adding also the rest: But not what I will, but what you will. But fleeing, how will you ask this, yourself granting yourself the removal of the cup, and not doing what the Father wills, but what you will?

choices.english: He himself also fled violence sometimes
choices.why: Keeps the concessive force of 'et ipse' (Christ himself, like others) and the literal 'vim' as violence, matching Tertullian's argument that Christ's withdrawals were temporary and purposeful.
rejected: He himself also escaped violence at times

choices.english: until of course he should fulfill his teaching
choices.why: Preserves 'scilicet' as an explanatory aside and 'impleret' as fulfill, showing the purpose-limit of the flight command.
rejected: until he had completed his doctrine
until he should finish his teaching

choices.english: I do not say he stood
choices.why: Keeps the rhetorical correction 'non dico' literally, showing Tertullian's intensification: not merely stood, but did not even seek help.
rejected: I will not say he stood

choices.why: Ablative absolute rendered as temporal clause; 'etiam' kept as 'even' to emphasize the extremity of refusing help.
rejected: rebuking even the sword of Peter

choices.why: Literal rendering of 'substantiam' as substance, preserving Tertullian's technical language about Christ's human nature (soul and flesh).
Keeps 'translationem' as removal/transfer, matching the prayer that the cup pass away, and avoids the glossary-banned 'escape'.

pass_b_english: He himself also fled violence sometimes, but for the same reason he had commanded the apostles to flee: until of course he should fulfill his teaching. Once that was completed, I do not say he stood, but he did not even seek help from the Father with armies of angels, after rebuking even Peter's sword. He confessed that his soul was anxious even to death and his flesh weak, to show you first that both human substances were in him—the anxiety of the soul and the weakness of the flesh—so that you would not interpret Christ's flesh or soul as something else, as some have now introduced. Then, having demonstrated their conditions, you would know that they are worth nothing by themselves without the Spirit. And so he puts forward the willing spirit, so that looking at the condition of each substance you may understand that the strength of the Spirit is also in you, just as the weakness of the flesh is, and from this you may know what to do from what and what to subject to what—the weak to the strong—so that you do not, as you now do, complain about the weakness of the flesh while ignoring the firmness of the Spirit. He also asked the Father that, if it were possible, the cup of suffering might pass from him. You too should ask, but standing as he did, asking only, and adding the rest: "Yet not what I will, but what you will". But if you flee, how will you ask this, when you yourself provide the removal of the cup, and do not what the Father wills, but what you will?
